To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the two types of cerebral representations of language are not modularity-based, and are not capable of interacting with each other, either directly or through a hypothetical interface, and that the increased activation observed in the neuroimaging literature when bilinguals are performing a second language task is not devoted to processing implicit linguistic competence, and is not a reflection of a hypothetical interface.

(1) implicit linguistic competence is not conscious, (2) it does not require conscious processing, (3) it is not modality specific, and (4) it is not amodal, and (5) it is not accessible to consciousness.

implicit linguistic competence is not capable of being converted into metalinguistic explicit knowledge, that the latter cannot be converted into the former, and that there can be no interface between the two.
In summary, our research is concerned with

a theory of the acquisition and representation of second languages that attempts to explain how the declarative and procedural aspects of memory contribute to the development of second language competence, how they interact with each other and with the first language, and what they contribute to the processing of a second and of the first language.
the declarative and procedural determinants of second languages, and the nature of the representations and processes involved in their acquisition and use.

a number of issues that have been central to the field of bilingualism for a number of years, and which have been addressed by many researchers, including, but not limited to: the role of explicit and implicit knowledge in bilingualism, the role of awareness in second language learning, the role of the interface in the bilingual brain and the role of the declarative and procedural memories in the representation and processing of language in the brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there is no interface between declarative and procedural memories, and that declarative knowledge of a second language, if it is acquired and maintained at all, is not capable of becoming implicit linguistic competence.
there is no interface between the two sets of representations.
declarative memory is the exclusive domain of metalinguistic and metacognitive knowledge, whereas procedural memory is the exclusive province of implicit linguistic competence.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the acquisition of second languages is a complex and fascinating phenomenon, but one that can only be fully explained by the interaction of a number of factors, some of them not even known to the learner, and some not even known to us.
declarative memory is the only source for the acquisition and representation of second languages.

the declarative/procedural dichotomy is a fundamental aspect of the organization of the human brain and that the same dichotomy is a key to the understanding of the nature of the bilingual brain and of the acquisition and representation of second languages.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the acquisition of a second language, as well as its ultimate attainment, is not a question of how much of the target language is acquired, but of how much of it is acquired implicitly.
the acquisition of a second language, like the acquisition of the first, is a matter of implicit learning and not of conscious learning.

there is an important distinction between declarative and procedural determinants of second language acquisition, and that this distinction is crucial to our understanding of second language learning, teaching and processing.
